title: Reasons for Action: Justification, Motivation, Explanation

summaries.example: Mia sees that her friend dropped a pencil. She has a reason to pick it up because helping is a point in favor of doing so. She may pick it up because she wants to help; that is her motivating reason. Someone might explain her action by saying she noticed the pencil. These are three ways reasons can connect with an action.
summaries.summary: When people ask what someone should do, why they did something, or what explains an action, they are asking about reasons. Philosophers often separate normative reasons, which count in favor of an action, from motivating reasons, which guide the person who acts. Explanatory reasons tell us why the action happened, and they may be different from both. For example, a person might be guided by a false belief, even though that belief does not really support the action. Philosophers also ask whether reasons are facts, thoughts, desires, or something else; how reasons are weighed; and whether acting for a good reason affects praise and responsibility.
key_ideas: Reasons can support an action, guide a person, or explain what happened.
A person can do the right thing for a poor reason, or do something based on a mistaken belief.
Reasons for and against an action may need to be compared.
Philosophers disagree about what reasons are and how they connect with thoughts, facts, and desires.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use reasons whenever we make choices, give advice, judge actions, or try to understand people. Thinking about reasons can help us separate what really supports an action from what merely caused someone to choose it. It also helps us ask fairer questions about mistakes, responsibility, and whether a good action was done for a good reason.

important_terms.definition: A fact or consideration that supports doing something.
The consideration that guides someone when they act.
A reason that helps us understand why an action happened.
Thinking carefully about what to do and comparing reasons for and against choices.

questions_to_think_about: Can a good reason guide you even if you do not know about it?
If someone helps only to get a prize, did they help for the best reason?
What should you do when one reason supports an action and another reason counts against it?

summaries.example: Suppose a student warns a classmate about a dangerous shortcut because the shortcut is unsafe. The danger is a normative reason against taking it, and it may also be the student’s motivating reason. But suppose the student gives the warning only because they expect public praise. The warning may still be useful, yet philosophers can ask whether the student acted for the moral reason that made helping important. The case separates doing what is right from acting for the right reason.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of practical reasons examines considerations connected with acting. A normative reason favors an action: it supports or justifies doing it and may contribute to an action’s deontic status. A motivating reason is what guides the agent, while an explanatory reason answers why the action occurred. These roles can coincide, but they need not. Someone may act on a false belief, or act for a self-interested motive while performing an action that another reason genuinely supports. The entry surveys competing views about the ontology of reasons, including fact-based, proposition-based, and mental-state accounts. It also considers how reasons guide deliberation, whether knowledge is required for acting in light of a fact, and whether all motivating reasons must appear to the agent as reasons in favor. Finally, it examines how reasons bear on responsibility, praise, and moral worth.
key_ideas: Normative, motivating, and explanatory roles may be played by one reason or by different reasons; the distinctions concern both function and, on some theories, what reasons are.
Normative reasons have a deontic role in determining what one ought or may do and a deliberative role in guiding thought about what to do.
Philosophers debate whether normative reasons are facts, how facts favor actions, and whether reasons depend on desires, value, rational deliberation, or none of these.
False beliefs create a problem for theories of motivating reasons: a person may act on an apparent fact that does not exist.
Some accounts require knowledge or another epistemic connection to a reason, while cases involving luck and misleading surroundings challenge that requirement.
The relation between acting for a normative reason and moral worth remains disputed; doing the right thing and doing it for the right reason may come apart.
summaries.why_it_matters: The distinctions matter across ethics, action theory, law, politics, and everyday judgment. They help explain why an action occurred without assuming that its cause justified it. They also clarify disagreements about rationality: what a person ought to do may depend on all the facts, while what the person could reasonably decide may depend on what they know or justifiably believe. Questions about acting for the right reasons connect practical reasoning with responsibility and credit.

important_terms.definition: A consideration that favors an action and can help determine what someone ought, must, or may do.
The consideration in light of which an agent acts; it is supposed to guide the action.
A consideration cited to make an action intelligible or to answer why it occurred; it need not favor the action.
The status of an action as required, permitted, or forbidden, often discussed as what one ought, must, or may do.
The view that motivating reasons are mental states, such as beliefs and desires.
The view that motivating reasons are facts, or alleged facts, rather than the agent’s mental states themselves.
The view that motivating reasons are propositions, including propositions that may be false but are believed by the agent.
The idea that an agent acts for a reason only if the consideration appears to support the action from the agent’s perspective.

questions_to_think_about: If a person acts on a false belief, is the false proposition their motivating reason, or only an apparent reason?
Should an unknown fact affect what someone ought to do, or only what they can reasonably be expected to do?
Can reasons be added together like weights, or can some reasons defeat, silence, or remain incomparable with others?
Does acting from a desire for praise make a helpful action less creditworthy?
Must intentional action involve taking some consideration to favor what one does?

summaries.example: Jordan studies for a test because the material interests him, but also because he wants a good grade. The importance of learning may be a normative reason to study, while his desire for a grade is a motivating reason. A teacher might explain the studying by pointing to Jordan’s belief that the test is tomorrow. If the test was actually next week, that belief still explains his choice, but it was a mistaken view of the situation.
summaries.summary: People ask for reasons in several connected but different ways. They may ask what favors an action, what led an agent to choose it, or what explains it afterward. Philosophers commonly call these normative, motivating, and explanatory reasons. A normative reason supports an action and can help determine whether it is required, allowed, or forbidden. A motivating reason guides the agent, but it need not actually support the action: someone can act from a false belief or from a selfish motive. The entry explores whether reasons are facts, propositions, or mental states, and whether the distinctions name different kinds of things or different jobs one reason can perform. It also examines how reasons guide deliberation, how we handle reasons we do not know, and why the reasons for which we act may affect responsibility and praise.
key_ideas: The word “reason” can answer different questions: What favors an action? What guided the agent? What explains the action?
Reasons for and against an action may conflict, so deciding what one ought to do is not always simple addition.
Normative reasons are often treated as facts, but philosophers disagree about whether facts are concrete things, true propositions, or something else.
Motivating reasons may involve facts, propositions, or mental states; mistaken actions make the choice among these theories difficult.
A person may act reasonably according to what they believe even when their belief is false, raising a difference between objective and subjective reasons.
Philosophers debate whether acting for a normative reason requires awareness, knowledge, a suitable desire, or a special kind of rational understanding.
summaries.why_it_matters: Understanding reasons helps us think more carefully about choices and judgments. It prevents us from confusing “this explains why someone acted” with “this makes the action a good idea.” The topic also matters when deciding whether a person acted rationally, whether a mistake was understandable, and whether doing the right thing deserves credit when the person acted from the wrong motive.

important_terms.definition: A consideration that counts in favor of a person’s doing something.
The reason that guides a person’s action from their point of view.
A consideration used to explain why an action happened, whether or not it supported the action.
Careful thinking about possible actions and the reasons for or against them.
A reason that supports an action to some extent but may be defeated by a stronger opposing reason.
A reason that appears to support an action but is based on a false belief or mistaken impression.
The view that reasons for action are facts or truths about the world.
The view that reasons for action are mental states, such as beliefs or desires.

questions_to_think_about: Is the reason that explains an action always the same as the reason that motivated it?
If a reason against an action is unknown to you, should it affect what you ought to do?
Can a false belief be a motivating reason, or does it only explain the action?
When two reasons conflict, should the stronger one always decide what you ought to do?
Is an action more praiseworthy when it is done for the reason that truly supports it?
